titre: A Thin Layer of Clay Tracked Down the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs
accroche: In 1980, a physicist and his geologist son find, in a layer of clay 66 million years old, a metal almost absent from the Earth's crust.
contenu_vulgarise:
Near Gubbio, in Italy's Umbria, a sequence of marine limestone has been piling up without interruption for more than a hundred million years, a geological book leafed layer by layer. In the middle of this stack, at the very spot where the fossils of foraminifera characteristic of the Cretaceous vanish all at once, a thin seam of clay barely a centimeter thick slips in. In 1977, the geologist Walter Alvarez takes samples there with no precise idea of what he is looking for. He hands them to his father Luis, a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, as well as to the chemists Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, specialists in neutron activation analysis, a technique capable of detecting elements in infinitesimal traces.

## An Element That Has No Business There

The result, published in 1980 in the journal *Science*, is clear: this thin layer of clay contains iridium in a quantity far above what is normally found in the Earth's crust. Iridium is a rare metal at the surface, having largely migrated to the core during the planet's formation, but it remains abundant in asteroids and comets, which never went through this internal differentiation. The Alvarez team draws from it a hypothesis that was radical for the time: an asteroid about ten kilometers in diameter struck the Earth 66 million years ago, exactly at the boundary where the fossils of non-avian dinosaurs stop. The dust thrown into the atmosphere would have blocked photosynthesis for months, collapsing food chains across the globe.

## The Crater Was Missing

The hypothesis convinces few, for lack of decisive proof: where is the crater? The answer already existed, but no one had made the connection. Geophysicists working for a Mexican oil company had spotted, as early as the 1970s, a circular structure buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula, near the village of Chicxulub, without understanding its origin. It is only in 1991 that the link with the iridium layer is established. The scientific debate then continues for nearly twenty years, some researchers favoring instead the role of the immense volcanic eruptions of the Deccan, in India, active during the same period.

## A Panel of Forty-One Researchers Settles It

In 2010, a panel of 41 scientists from several countries reviews twenty years of accumulated data, sedimentology, climate modeling, precise datings, and concludes in *Science* that the Chicxulub impact remains the main cause of the extinction: Deccan volcanism, active over several hundred thousand years, produced only disturbances too gradual to explain so abrupt a disappearance, concentrated exactly at the geological boundary. A centimeter of Italian clay had sufficed, thirty years earlier, to point in the right direction, before anyone had identified where the responsible object had ended up landing.

repere.texte: In 2010, a panel of 41 researchers gathered around Peter Schulte reviews twenty years of data and confirms, in the journal Science, that the Chicxulub impact, an asteroid about 10 to 15 km in diameter, remains the main cause of the Cretaceous extinction, 66 million years ago.
repere.source: Schulte et al., Science, 2010 — via Jackson School of Geosciences, UT Austin

carte.punch: One centimeter of clay was enough to track down the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.
carte.idee: In 1980, a team led by the physicist Luis Alvarez finds, in a thin layer of clay 66 million years old, a concentration of iridium far too high to come from Earth, the signature of an asteroid impact. It will take eleven years to locate the crater, in Mexico.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Complete timeline of the debate, from the 1980 discovery to the identification of the Chicxulub crater in 1991.

quiz.question: Why did the presence of iridium in the clay layer put the Alvarezes on the trail of an extraterrestrial impact rather than a purely terrestrial cause?
choix: Because iridium exists nowhere else but in meteorites
Because iridium is rare at the Earth's surface but abundant in asteroids and comets
Because iridium forms only during a mass extinction
Because iridium had already been found in the Chicxulub crater
quiz.explication: Iridium largely migrated to the Earth's core during the planet's formation, which makes it rare at the surface, but asteroids and comets, which are undifferentiated, contain far more of it. This imbalance points to an extraterrestrial origin. The Chicxulub crater was only linked to this layer in 1991, eleven years after the discovery of the anomaly.

choix: Luis Alvarez, a Nobel Prize-winning physicist
Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, chemists

quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that the chemists Frank Asaro and Helen Michel were specialists in neutron activation analysis, a technique capable of detecting elements in infinitesimal traces.

choix: Geophysicists working for a Mexican oil company
The team of Walter and Luis Alvarez

quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that geophysicists working for a Mexican oil company had spotted this structure as early as the 1970s, without understanding its origin; the link with the iridium layer was only established in 1991.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the panel of 41 researchers conclude in 2010 about Deccan volcanism?
choix: That it produced disturbances too gradual to explain so abrupt an extinction
That it is the main cause of the extinction, ahead of the Chicxulub impact
That it had no measurable effect on the climate of the time
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The panel concludes in Science that Deccan volcanism, active over several hundred thousand years, produced disturbances too gradual to explain so abrupt a disappearance, concentrated at the geological boundary.
